listenings.text: Every year we receive more than three hundred speaker bios, and most of them have the same problem. They are lists. Born in, studied at, worked at, worked at, worked at. Nobody reads a list. A good bio tells a short story with a clear line. Start with what the speaker does today, not with the university. Then choose two or three moments that explain the career: an appointment, a turnaround, a difficult decision. Write them as events, not as a sequence of verbs. For example, instead of he was appointed CEO and he restructured the company, write: his appointment as CEO led to the restructuring of the company. It is shorter, and it sounds more professional. And please, keep it under one hundred words.

People always ask me why I left a career as a CEO to go back to law. The short answer is that I missed the questions more than the answers. During my tenure as CEO, the company went through a difficult turnaround. We sold two businesses and rebuilt the rest. It was a great experience, but I realized that the part I enjoyed most was the regulatory side: the negotiations with the agencies, the drafting of the rules. So after the sale of the company, I made the decision to return to practice. I also started my doctorate, which was a dream from my university years. Looking back, the transition was the best decision of my career.

reading.rtitle: The Bio Nobody Reads, and the One Everybody Remembers
paras: At every international conference, the audience reads the speaker bios before the panel begins. Most of these bios are forgotten in seconds. They are lists of verbs: he studied, he worked, he joined, he was appointed. Communication consultants say the problem is not the content. It is the form. A list of actions does not tell a story, and without a story, the reader has nothing to remember.

The bios that people remember use a different technique: they turn actions into events. Instead of he was appointed CEO in 2015 and he restructured the company, the writer says: his appointment as CEO in 2015 led to the restructuring of the company. The nouns appointment and restructuring become the subjects of the story. This is called nominalization, and it is typical of professional and academic English. It makes a text shorter, more formal, and easier to scan.

Nominalization has limits. Too many nouns in one sentence make a bio dense and cold, and a reader can lose track of who did what. The best bios mix the two forms: nouns for the key events, such as an appointment, a turnaround or a transition, and simple verbs for the rest. A good test is to read the bio aloud. If it sounds like a legal document, use more verbs. If it sounds like a list, use more nouns.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B1 reading, written for this lesson from common advice by communication consultants and conference organizers

Memorable bios turn key actions into events with nouns, but they still mix nouns and verbs.
